subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which physical factor tends to give a LOW population density?
options: High, rugged mountains with a harsh climate
Temperate climate with reliable rainfall
Flat coastal lowland
Fertile river valley
questions.explain: Steep mountains, thin soils and harsh climates make farming and settlement difficult, leading to sparse populations.

questions.q: In a typical urban land-use pattern, which area is usually found at the centre of a city?
options: Open countryside
The Central Business District (CBD)
Heavy industry only
Low-density suburbs
questions.explain: The CBD is the commercial heart of a city, with shops and offices, usually located in the centre where land is most accessible.

questions.q: What is a 'squatter settlement' (slum)?
options: An area of poor-quality housing built illegally on unused land
A modern business district
A protected green belt area
A planned suburb with large houses
questions.explain: Squatter settlements, such as favelas, are areas of self-built, often illegal housing that lack basic services.

questions.q: Heavy traffic congestion in a growing city mainly leads to:
options: Air pollution and longer journey times
A fall in the city's population
Faster commuting for everyone
Cleaner air and lower emissions
questions.explain: Congestion increases air pollution from exhaust fumes and wastes time, harming health and the economy.

questions.q: One way to improve a squatter settlement is through 'site and service' schemes, which:
options: Move all residents to rural areas
Provide land with basic utilities so residents can build better homes
Demolish the settlement entirely
Ban residents from making improvements
questions.explain: Site and service schemes give people a plot connected to water and electricity, allowing them to gradually self-build improved housing.

questions.q: What does 'urban regeneration' mean?
options: Improving and renewing run-down urban areas
Moving a city to a new location
Demolishing a city completely
Building new cities in the countryside
questions.explain: Urban regeneration is the redevelopment and improvement of derelict or run-down parts of a city, such as old docklands.

questions.q: In Stage 1 of the Demographic Transition Model, the population is stable because:
options: Both rates are very low
Birth rate is high but death rate is very low
Migration balances the numbers
Both birth rate and death rate are high
questions.explain: In Stage 1 high birth rates are cancelled out by high death rates, so total population stays low and fluctuating.

questions.q: A dispersed settlement pattern is one where:
options: Buildings are tightly clustered together
Buildings follow a road in a line
All houses are in one block
Buildings are spread out and isolated
questions.explain: In a dispersed pattern, settlements are scattered and isolated, often in remote or upland farming areas.

questions.q: Recycling household waste and using renewable energy in a city helps make it more sustainable by:
options: Raising air pollution levels
Increasing the use of landfill
Reducing waste and lowering carbon emissions
Using up more fossil fuels
questions.explain: Recycling cuts the waste sent to landfill and renewable energy lowers carbon emissions, improving sustainability.

questions.q: In Stage 2 of the Demographic Transition Model, population grows rapidly because:
options: Birth rate stays high while death rate falls
Both rates are high and stable
Birth rate falls sharply
Death rate rises above birth rate
questions.explain: In Stage 2 death rates drop due to better healthcare and food while birth rates remain high, causing rapid growth.

questions.q: The 'situation' of a settlement refers to its:
options: Physical land it is built on
Main economic function
Total population size
Position relative to surrounding features and other places
questions.explain: Situation describes where a settlement lies in relation to its surroundings, such as routes, rivers and other towns.

questions.q: What is the main reason rural-urban migration leads to rapid city growth in many LICs and NEEs?
options: Birth rates in cities are extremely low
People move from countryside to city seeking jobs and a better life
Cities are losing population to the countryside
City death rates are higher than rural ones
questions.explain: Large numbers of people migrate from rural areas to cities in search of work, services and opportunities, swelling urban populations.

questions.q: Which feature is typical of a youthful population pyramid?
options: Straight vertical sides
An equal width at every age
A wide base and narrow top
A narrow base and wide top
questions.explain: A youthful population has many children and few elderly, giving a pyramid with a wide base that narrows towards the top.

questions.q: Why do many of the wealthier residents in UK cities live in the suburbs rather than the inner city?
options: Suburbs are the cheapest place to live
Suburbs often have more space, greener surroundings and newer housing
There are no roads in the inner city
Inner cities have no jobs at all
questions.explain: Suburbs typically offer larger, newer homes with gardens and a quieter environment, attracting wealthier families.

questions.q: A 'green belt' around a UK city is an area of land that is:
options: Protected from most building to limit urban sprawl
Used only for car parks
Reserved for new factories
The busiest shopping district
questions.explain: A green belt is protected open land around a city that restricts development and helps prevent urban sprawl.

questions.q: What is the difference between a refugee and an economic migrant?
options: There is no difference
An economic migrant is forced to flee persecution
A refugee always moves for a better job
A refugee is forced to flee, an economic migrant moves to seek work
questions.explain: Refugees are forced to leave to escape danger such as war or persecution, whereas economic migrants move to improve their living standards.

questions.q: Which of these cities is a megacity in a newly emerging economy (NEE)?
options: Oslo, Norway
Cardiff, Wales
Mumbai, India
Reykjavik, Iceland
questions.explain: Mumbai is a rapidly growing megacity in India, a newly emerging economy.

questions.q: Natural increase in a population occurs when:
options: Birth rate is higher than death rate
Death rate is higher than birth rate
Migration into a country rises
The population stays the same
questions.explain: Natural increase is when births exceed deaths, causing the population to grow before migration is considered.

questions.q: A megacity is usually defined as a city with a population of more than:
options: 1 million
500 million
10 million
questions.explain: A megacity is an urban area with a population of over 10 million people.

questions.q: Population density is best defined as:
options: The number of people per unit area
The total number of people in a country
The number of births each year
How quickly a population grows
questions.explain: Population density measures how many people live in a given area, usually expressed as people per square kilometre.

questions.q: Which statement about megacities is correct today?
options: An increasing number of the world's megacities are in LICs and NEEs
Most megacities are now in richer, developed countries
Megacities have stopped growing everywhere
There are no megacities in Asia
questions.explain: Megacity growth is now fastest in LICs and NEEs, with many of the largest cities found in Asia and Africa.

questions.q: Which of these is a social challenge linked to rapid urban growth?
options: Falling demand for healthcare
Inequality between rich and poor districts
An end to overcrowding
Reduced crime in all areas
questions.explain: Rapid urban growth often widens inequality, with wealthy areas alongside deprived slums lacking services.
